Day and night: take a turn with Earth

Use a lamp and a globe to separate Earth’s daily rotation from its yearly journey around the Sun.

By Biel Sardà · Published 1 Oct 2026 · Suggest a correction

Keep the lamp still

Imagine a globe beside a lamp in a dark room. The side facing the lamp is lit. The side facing away is in shadow. Put a small sticker on the globe and slowly turn it.

When the sticker faces the light, its place is in daytime. When it turns away, that place is in nighttime. The Sun does not need to circle Earth every day for this change to happen: Earth rotates.

Try it yourself

Turn the marker around the simplified Earth below. The light always arrives from the left. Notice when the marker enters the lit half and when it moves into the dark half.

The drawing is a model, not a live map or a sunrise forecast. It leaves out latitude, the atmosphere and the tilt of Earth. Those details affect real daylight, but the simple model makes the daily turning easier to see.

A spin and a journey

A rotation is a turn around an axis, like the globe spinning on its stand. An orbit is a journey around another object. Earth rotates while it also travels around the Sun.

A solar day is about 24 hours; Earth’s trip around the Sun takes about a year. Mixing up these two motions makes it hard to explain why night happens every day while seasons change over months.

Why someone else is awake

Two places on different sides of Earth do not face the Sun at the same time. Your evening can be someone else’s morning. Clock systems help people organise this difference, but the turning Earth comes first.

Next, move the lamp-and-ball idea to the Moon. Half of the Moon is normally lit by the Sun too, yet the amount of that lit half visible from Earth changes through the month.
